He hears Paul address Kountze directly, tell him that he was born lucky, and lecture him about privilege he did not earn. Smith therefore receives Paul’s opinion firsthand as Paul expresses it to Kountze in the dining hall. He does not learn it from another student recounting Paul’s remarks later.

Smith hears Paul lecture Kountze about Kountze's unearned privilege.
Smith witnesses Paul's statement to Kountze firsthand.
Smith does not learn Paul's view from another student's later recounting.

questions.question: At the infirmary farewell, how had Park’s understanding of Angus developed, in order?
questions.answer: At first, Park believes Angus is among the holdovers because Angus’s planned St. Kitts vacation has been canceled. Later, Angus directly tells Park that he has already been expelled from three schools. In the infirmary, Angus also tells Park that he suffers from nightmares involving falling or drowning. After Park discloses his accident, Angus offers to help conceal the soiled sheets the next morning so Park can avoid discovery.

Park learns directly from Angus about Angus’s previous expulsions.
Angus tells Park that Angus suffers from nightmares.
Angus offers to conceal Park’s accident.

questions.question: In their hotel room, how do Angus and Paul each understand the pills?
questions.answer: Angus knows that his pills are not vitamins, but he lies to Paul by describing them as vitamins for low energy. Paul recognizes the pills as Librium. After Angus goes into the bathroom, Paul retrieves his own bottle of Librium, which is identical to Angus’s bottle.

claims.text: Angus knows that his pills are not vitamins.
Angus lies to Paul about his pills.
Paul recognizes the pills as Librium.
Paul retrieves his own bottle, which is identical to Angus’s.

questions.question: Alone with Angus in the administrative office hallway, when does Paul reconsider calling?
questions.answer: Paul Hunham reconsiders only after Angus Tully suggests that the family may have returned. Until then, Paul regards another call as pointless because the desk clerk had said the family was away. Angus’s suggestion is the turning point: Paul accepts that possibility and changes his mind about calling. He has not acquired any new firsthand evidence that they are back; the reconsideration rests on Angus’s suggestion.

claims.text: Paul Hunham initially considers another call pointless because the desk clerk said the family was away.
Angus Tully suggests that the family may have returned.
Paul Hunham changes his mind about calling in response to Angus Tully’s suggestion.

questions.question: In the headmaster's office, with the snow globe on the desk, what does Judy make of Paul's account of the Boston excursion?
questions.answer: Judy accepts that Paul took Angus to Boston over the holidays, but she does not accept his description of the excursion as an authorized academic field trip. She recognizes the snow globe as an item confiscated from Angus’s father at the sanitarium after Angus gave it to him. To Judy, that origin exposes Paul’s academic-field-trip account as a cover story for Angus’s visit to his father.

claims.text: Judy accepts that Paul took Angus to Boston over the holidays.
Judy recognizes that the snow globe came from Angus's father at the sanitarium.
The snow globe's origin exposes Paul's authorized academic field-trip claim to Judy as a cover story.

questions.question: At the hospital pharmacy, how does Angus learn Paul's terms for their arrangement?
questions.answer: Paul tells Angus the terms directly: their arrangement must remain strictly confidential, and Angus must not exploit the situation for personal gain.

claims.text: Paul tells Angus that their arrangement must remain strictly confidential.
Paul warns Angus not to use the situation for personal gain.

questions.question: In the movie-theatre balcony, what destination do Angus and Paul each expect for Angus?
questions.answer: Angus knows that he is leaving the theater through the front doors. He tells Paul that he is going to the bathroom, using the bathroom as a pretext for his departure. Paul believes that Angus is headed to the bathroom and acknowledges Angus’s announcement with a nod. Thus, Angus’s intended destination differs from the destination Paul expects.

claims.text: Angus knows he is leaving the theater through the front doors.
Angus uses the bathroom as a pretext.
Paul believes Angus is going to the bathroom.
Paul acknowledges Angus’s announcement with a nod.

questions.question: In Angus’s dorm room, what does Kountze make of Angus’s claims about the cigarettes and marijuana sale?
questions.answer: Kountze rejects Angus Tully’s denial that Angus stole the cigarettes, and Kountze continues to maintain the accusation that Angus stole them. Kountze also rejects Angus Tully’s two claims about the marijuana sale. Kountze does not accept that the marijuana is poor quality, and Kountze does not accept that the marijuana is overpriced. Thus, Kountze rejects both Angus’s quality judgment and Angus’s price judgment.

claims.text: Kountze rejects Angus Tully’s denial that Angus Tully stole the cigarettes.
Kountze maintains the accusation that Angus Tully stole the cigarettes.
Kountze rejects Angus Tully’s claim that the marijuana is poor quality.
Kountze rejects Angus Tully’s claim that the marijuana is overpriced.

questions.question: On the open highway, what had Tressler learned about the Walk, in order?
questions.answer: First, Tressler accepts the Major’s stated rule: after three warnings, a walker receives a ticket. Later, Tressler learns that radio reception is available in the area after all. He then learns what a ticket means: violent execution. Through that discovery, Tressler also learns that the soldiers enforce the Walk’s rules brutally, rather than treating the announced penalties as merely abstract rules.

claims.text: Tressler accepts the Major’s stated rule that three warnings bring a ticket.
Tressler learns that radio reception is available in the area after all.
Tressler learns that a ticket means violent execution.
Tressler learns that the soldiers brutally enforce the Walk’s rules.

questions.question: In the Garraty kitchen, how does Ginnie gauge her family's response to her singing?
questions.answer: Ginnie gauges her family’s response through Raymond and William’s words, as well as William’s behavior. Raymond directly reveals his reaction by insisting that she keep singing. William tells her that he also enjoys her singing, giving her a second verbal measure of its reception. His affectionate kiss supplies further behavioral reinforcement, confirming the positive response he has already expressed aloud.

claims.text: Raymond insists that Ginnie keep singing.
William says that he also enjoys Ginnie's singing.
William reinforces his positive response to Ginnie's singing with an affectionate kiss.

questions.question: At the 100-mile town, what does Garraty learn and believe about the Walk?
questions.answer: Garraty learns directly from the Major that the walkers have reached 100 miles and that a prize awaits the eventual winner. Garraty accepts that the winner will receive a prize. He also takes the Walk’s lethal stakes seriously, regarding death as a genuine consequence. Likewise, Garraty takes the prohibition on fleeing seriously after seeing its enforcement.

claims.text: Garraty accepts the Major’s claim that the eventual winner will receive a prize.
Garraty learns the 100-mile and prize claims directly from the Major.
Garraty takes the Walk’s lethal stakes seriously.
Garraty takes the prohibition on fleeing seriously.

questions.question: At the 100-mile mark, what makes Barkovitch rethink the warning rules?
questions.answer: At the 100-mile mark, another walker runs toward the diner. Soldiers immediately execute that walker, and Barkovitch witnesses the execution firsthand. The event leads Barkovitch to realize that fleeing the road can result in immediate execution. The basis for his realization is therefore the walker’s run toward the diner and the soldiers’ immediate lethal response, which Barkovitch personally witnesses.

claims.text: Another walker runs toward the diner.
Soldiers immediately execute the walker who runs toward the diner.
Barkovitch witnesses the walker's immediate execution firsthand.
Barkovitch realizes that fleeing the road can mean immediate execution.

questions.question: On the open road through the expansive field, how has Garraty's view of Collie Parker evolved?
questions.answer: Garraty and Collie Parker’s relationship becomes personally antagonistic. When Parker threatens violent retaliation for Garraty’s remarks, Garraty sees that Parker is prepared to answer him with violence. Later, on the road through the expansive field, Garraty accepts the pact forbidding assistance among the walkers, including assistance between Garraty and Parker. Parker also explicitly accepts that same non-assistance pact.

claims.text: Garraty and Collie Parker's relationship becomes personally antagonistic.
Garraty sees Collie Parker as ready to answer Garraty with violence.
Garraty accepts the pact forbidding assistance between Garraty and Collie Parker.
Collie Parker accepts the pact forbidding assistance between Garraty and Collie Parker.

questions.question: At the 100-mile town, how does Collie Parker know Baker understands the penalty for leaving the route?
questions.answer: Collie Parker knows Baker understands because he and Arthur Baker witness the same walker run toward the diner and be shot by soldiers. The immediate shooting shows both men that fleeing can bypass the usual warning sequence. Since Baker sees that consequence alongside Collie, Collie has direct evidence that Baker has understood the penalty. The Major’s subsequent lecture reinforces what they have just witnessed.

claims.text: Collie Parker and Arthur Baker witness soldiers shoot the same walker who runs toward the diner.
The shooting shows Collie Parker and Arthur Baker that fleeing can bypass the usual warning sequence.
The Major’s subsequent lecture reinforces what Collie Parker and Arthur Baker have witnessed.

questions.question: At the 100-mile town, what does Baker make of Stebbins’ explanations?
questions.answer: At the 100-mile town, Baker accepts Stebbins’ explanation that crowds are restricted until the finish, responding in terms of the possibility that Stebbins may never see one. Baker also witnesses Stebbins’ coughing fit. When Stebbins explains that the Major sleeps after dinner and even showers, Baker accepts that account too, reacting that the arrangement is unfair.

claims.text: Baker accepts Stebbins’ explanation that crowds are restricted until the finish.
Baker accepts Stebbins’ explanation that the Major sleeps and showers normally at night.
Baker sees Stebbins’ coughing fit.

questions.question: In the deserted village, how does Olson form his view of Barkovitch’s survival strategy?
questions.answer: Barkovitch addresses the walkers while Olson is present. Olson hears Barkovitch explain that the walkers need focus and a plan, then declare that he himself has a plan. Thus, Olson has direct testimony from Barkovitch about Barkovitch’s claimed survival strategy, and this testimony provides the basis for Olson’s view of that strategy.

claims.text: Barkovitch addresses the walkers.
Olson hears Barkovitch say that Barkovitch has a plan.
Olson is present for Barkovitch’s remarks.
Olson bases his view on direct testimony from Barkovitch.

questions.question: At the field picnic, what does McVries make of Garraty’s account of the spectators?
questions.answer: McVries rejects Garraty’s account. Specifically, he rejects Garraty’s characterization of the spectators as animals eager to see a violent death. McVries insists that Garraty recognize the picnickers as human beings, rather than reduce them to that image. His insistence also has a personal effect on Garraty: it makes Garraty question his own motives. That is the challenge McVries poses to Garraty at the picnic.

claims.text: McVries rejects Garraty’s characterization of the spectators as animals eager to see violent death.
McVries insists that Garraty recognize the picnickers’ humanity.
McVries’s insistence on the picnickers’ humanity makes Garraty question Garraty’s motives.

questions.question: In the Garratys’ front yard, how does the Major learn William’s position on the state’s offer?
questions.answer: In the front yard, the Major learns William Garraty’s position firsthand. The Major personally presents William with the state’s choice between lifetime service and deactivation. William then refuses to make the allegiance pledge despite the stated consequences, and the Major directly witnesses that refusal. William’s refusal in the Major’s presence is how the Major discovers that William will not accept the state’s offer.

claims.text: The Major personally presents William Garraty with the choice between lifetime service and deactivation.
William Garraty refuses the allegiance pledge despite its consequences.
The Major directly witnesses William Garraty’s refusal.
